text: DARBISHRE, — On July 4, 1926,

label: paragraph_title
text: DEATHS.

label: text
text: From the report of the case in the Supreme Court in which Capt. J. M. Anderson was unsuccessful in his case against the Man Wing Steamship Company for the payment of three months' wages in lieu of reasonable notice, it is clear that the status of master mariners on Chinese owned steamers leaves very much to be desired. In the particular case mentioned the Court decided against the plaintiff, and it is not for us to question that judgment.

label: paragraph_title
text: Hongkong, Friday, July 16, 1926.

label: text
text: What must be assailed, however, is the practice of engaging master mariners with the implied or mutually agreed condition of liability to dismissal at twenty-four hours' notice. Although Captain Anderson did not agree with him, Mr. Jenkin, as counsel for the shipping company in question, suggested that it is the custom on China Coasters to employ masters at twenty-four hours' notice. Moreover, he pointed out that "the Company had always considered it of prime importance to get their officers on 24 hours' notice terms." In that case this particular company and any other Chinese company with similar views ought to be thoroughly ashamed of themselves to make such a confession. The point was also emphasised that when Captain Anderson was engaged as master there were many men with masters' tickets unemployed, this being more in evidence since the Seamen's Strike of 1922. What on earth this has got to do with engaging a master mariner with the right of 24 hours' notice of dismissal is not clear. It looks like taking advantage of the state of the labour market to secure qualified men and place on them great responsibilities on any old terms. If a man is out of a billet, no matter what his qualifications may be, he can be offered terms on a level with unskilled cooler labour. Apparently it is not worth anyone looking on the Mercantile Marine as a profession.

label: paragraph_title
text: 24 HOURS NOTICE

label: text
text: so far as Chinese owned vessels are concerned. Hundreds of pounds may be spent on working one's way from the bottom of the ladder to the position of chief command of a vessel, only to find that employment on a Chinese owned vessel is impossible unless one agrees to the condition of getting the order of the boot without rhyme or reason at twenty-four hours' notice. And the Chinese shipping companies prate that they consider this of "prime importance" in getting officers to work for them.

label: text
text: One need, not be a staunch Trade Unionist or an adherent of the Labour Party to condemn this system of twenty-four hours' notice as inimical to the best interests of the master mariners, and of the shipping companies, as well as of the travelling public who entrust their lives to their safe keeping. Human nature is human nature all the world over, and where will you find a master mariner who will put his whole heart and soul into his duties knowing that he is liable at any time to have his career blasted and his reputation damaged—perhaps for ever—by receiving twenty-four hours' notice of dismissal? In what other profession would such an intolerant and vexatious condition be imposed? It is not enough to say that because one man accepts such a condition without civil others should do the same. The whole principle is utterly wrong and grossly unfair to the whole Mercantile Marine, and the sooner the Mercantile Guard and the China Coast Officers' Guild get busy and secure more honourable terms for its members in the employment of Chinese companies the better. They will at least be assured of the strong support of the general public of this Colony.

label: paragraph_title
text: CAPT. MacINTOSH.

label: text
text: "LEAVES FOR HOME AFTER TREATMENT."

label: text
text: Capt., W. MacIntosh of the pirated s.s. "Tungchow," (seized in January last by Cantonese pirates near Weihaiwei, taken to Bias Bay and then abandoned) is leaving for Home.

label: text
text: Capt. MacIntosh, is one of the China Navigation Co.'s best-known shippers, and he left Shanghai last week for England on the P. & O. a.s. "Karmala." He had to have a foot amputated, as a result of the wound he received when the ship was seized.

label: text
text: The pirates tried to compel Capt. McIntosh to surrender. He refused to do so. As a consequence, the pirates shot at him, and Capt. MacIntosh has been in hospital practically ever since having his wounds treated.

label: text
text: Three men arrested on a B. & S. boat later and identified as members of the pirate gang went to their death recently before a firing squad in the native city at Shanghai.

label: paragraph_title
text: ANOTHER SHOOTING.

label: paragraph_title
text: RUNAWAY SHOT BY A DETECTIVE.

label: text
text: CORONER'S INQUIRY

label: text
text: An inquiry into the death of a Chinese from a bullet wound inflicted by a detective on the night of June 26 commenced before Mr. R. E. Lindsell and a jury at the Central Magistracy yesterday afternoon. The deceased was alleged to be one of four suspicious characters who ran away from the detective when he accustomed them.

label: text
text: sell related the circumstances of the affair and said it would be for them to decide whether the shooting was justifiable or not. Dr. Craig in his medical evidence said that he found three bullet wounds on the body, one of which pierced the liver and intestines. The first and third shots were apparently fired from behind and the other was fired from the front. Death was due to shock and haemorrhage caused by the wounds.

label: text
text: The Chinese mortuary attendant gave evidence of picking up a spent bullet which fell out of the dead man's clothing. He also deposed to finding a canvas knife sheath inside the socks.

label: text
text: Further evidence was to the effect that the detective gave chase and shots were fired by the detective at the runaway who dropped dead near the Central Market. When the dead body was taken to the Police Station, a dagger was found among the man's clothing.

label: text
text: The inquiry was adjourned until to-day for the evidence of the detective.

label: text
text: the owners at yesterday afternoon's hearing of the case in which Mr. J. M. Anderson, master mariner, claimed $1,515 from the Man Wing Steamship Company as wages in lieu of notice of termination of a verbal agreement for his captaincy of the s.s. Haitian, Mr. F. C. Jenkins dealt with the element of hardship which might appear on the face of things. He would like to point out, though, he said, that Mr. Anderson by the fortuitous fact that Capt. Jones went home on private affairs in 1924 stepped into a job whereby his salary was doubled for a period of ten months.

label: text
text: Mr. Jenkin said it was inconceivable that, although Mr. Anderson was working on the same ship as Capt. Jones and was a very great personal friend of his, he was not aware of the conditions of Capt. Jones's employment whereby he could be dismissed at 24 hours notice.

label: text
text: He also asked the court to disregard the statement that had the matter of 24 hours notice been broached Capt. Anderson would not have accepted the terms of the agreement. There was evidence before the court that he was on a 24 hours agreement with the same firm at $320 a month. Would he have refused a job on the same terms of determination at a salary about double that?

label: paragraph_title
text: "Remarkable Version."

label: text
text: His Lordship in delivering judgment said Captain Anderson's version of the interview was remarkable because one would have thought that there would have been discussion of terms of employment. It was also remarkable that in handing Captain Anderson a letter dismissing him at 24 hours notice, he should have offered him a month's salary in lieu of notice. In the first correspondence between the solicitors there was no mention of this. The first letter from the plaintiffs was to the effect that the claim was for wrongful dismissal and that Captain Anderson was entitled to three months' notice. It was remarkable if the solicitors had known of this that they should not have mentioned it in their letters. Had they done so it would have strengthened plaintiff's case.

label: text
text: Captain Jones, whose place plaintiff took, was in fact on an agreement determinable at 24 hours notice and he found it difficult to understand how, when the four men met, Captain Anderson was not in possession of this information.

label: text
text: It was to him a matter of regret that neither side had called Captain Jones.

label: text
text: The question of 24 hours notice was evidently present in the mind of Chan and it appeared reasonable to suppose that this important matter was mentioned at the interview. He came to that conclusion without finding that Captain Anderson had deliberately attempted to deceive the court, because the meeting seemed to have been short and informal and it was possible that the plaintiff did not fully apprehend all that took place.

label: text
text: He entered judgment for deendants, with costs.

label: text
text: A GRAVE DOUBT:

label: text
text: Before Major C. Willson at the Central Magistracy yesterday, a Chinese timber merchant was charged with being in possession of three forged ten-dollar bank notes.

label: text
text: Evidence was given of defendant's arrests with the notes in his possession when about to board the s.s. "Kinshan" for Macao.

label: text
text: Mr. M. K. Lo, who appeared for the defence; said that the notes were given to the defendant by a friend in Canton. On his arrival in Hongkong defendant found that the notes were forged and decided to take them back to Canton. Mr. Lo submitted that there had been no intention of uttering the notes in Hongkong.

label: text
text: His Worship held there was a grave doubt in the case and discharged the defendant.

label: paragraph_title
text: FIRST COURT OF THE SEASON.

label: paragraph_title
text: "A. THOUSAND ROYAL GUESTS."

label: text
text: Women in dresses that sparkled with diamonds and pearls, and men in uniforms glittering with orders and decorations, passed before the King and Queen when their Majesties held their first Court of the season at Buckingham Palace.

label: text
text: The Scots Guards posted a guard of honour with band in the palace quadrangle; the picturesque Gentlemen-at-Arms supplied the Throne Guard; their cordon facing towards the throne dais, and the Yeomen of the Guard, the King's Marshal Men, and troopers of the Household Cavalry were on duty at their accustomed stations.

label: text
text: The King wore the uniform of Colonel-in-Chief of the Royal Horse Guards, with the ribands of the Carter and Bath and numerous decorations.

label: text
text:
Queen in Silver Tissue.
The Queen was splendidly dressed in a gown of silver tissue with an overdress of tulle, embroidered with pearls and silver paillette. The train was of Irish point lace lined with silver. Her Majesty wore as heddress a Russian-shaped diamond, tara. Her other ornaments included the lesser Stars of Africa and other diamond embellishments together with the Order of the Garter and sundry family orders.

label: text
text: The Royal circle, which was somewhat smaller than usual, comprised the Duke of York, the Duke of Connaught, Prince and Princess Arthur of Connaught, Princess Helena Victoria, the Marquis and Marchioness of Cambridge, Prince Chichibu of Japan, and Prince Gustaf Adolf, Duke of Vasterbotten.

label: text
text: Just before ten o'clock their Majesties entered the White drawing-room and a procession was formed to the ball-room, where the King and Queen took their places at the front of the throne dais with the royal relatives grouped behind them.

label: paragraph_title
text: 1,000 Guests.

label: text
text: As is the custom at the opening, Court of the season, the guests —numbering about 1,000—were drawn mainly from Government, Diplomatic, and other official circles.

label: text
text: Beefeaters and other officials opened the gates to them at 8.30, and others ushered them from the ante-rooms towards the Throne.

label: text
text: The Lord Chamberlain announced the name of each debutante, who found herself in a Throne Room radiant with lofty palms, and banks of flowers in which half-open roses predominated.

label: text
text: The state rooms were beautifully decorated with flowers, and music was provided by a Guards band.
